(p-232) The second: A group of Quraysh went out on a trading journey to the land of the Negus (al-Najāshī). They stopped beside a church, lit a fire, and roasted meat. When they departed, the wind blew, and the place caught fire. The Negus became angry on account of the church, and his senior companions — among them Ḥijr ibn Sharāḥīl and Abū Yaksūm — said to him, "Do not grieve; we will demolish the Ka'bah." This was related by Muqātil. Ibn Isḥāq said: Abū Yaksūm's name was Abraha ibn al-Ashram. It is also said that he was his vizier, and Ḥijr was one of his commanders.

Mention of the reference to the story

The people of tafsir (exegesis) mentioned that when Abraha marched with his troops toward the Ka'bah to demolish it, he went out with the elephant. When he drew near to Mecca, he ordered his companions to raid the camels of the people, and they seized camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib. He sent one of his soldiers and said, "Ask about the chief of Mecca and inform him that I have not come to fight; I have only come to demolish this House." He has come only to demolish this House, and then he will depart from you." 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib said, "We have no fight with him, and we have no power against him. We will leave between him and what he came for, for this is the Sacred House of God and the House of His friend Abraham, peace be upon him. If He protects it, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between him and that, then by God we have no strength against it." He said, "Then come with me to the king." When 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib entered upon Abraha, Abraha held him in high esteem and honored him. Then he said to his interpreter, "Say to him: What is your need of the king?" The interpreter spoke to him, and he said, "My need is that he return to me two hundred camels that he took from me."

(p-233) Abraha said to his interpreter, "Say to him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but now I have lost my regard for you. I came to a House which is your religion so that I might demolish it, and you did not speak to me about it, yet you speak to me about camels I have taken." 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib said, "I am the lord of these camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it." So he ordered that his camels be returned to him. He went out and informed Quraysh, and commanded them to scatter in the ravines and on the mountain tops out of fear of the harm of the army when it entered. They did so. Then 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib came to the Ka'bah, took hold of the ring of the door, and began to say:

"O Lord, I do not hope for anyone other than You;
O Lord, protect them from Your sanctuary.
Indeed, the enemy of the House is one who opposes You;
Keep them from ruining Your sanctuary."

He also said:

"O God, a man defends his camp,
so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross prevail,
nor their stratagem against Your stratagem tomorrow.

(p-234) They have dragged all their lands
and the elephant, that they may take captive your people.
They have targeted your sanctuary with their plotting
out of ignorance, and they did not regard your majesty.
If You are leaving them and our Ka'bah,
then it is a matter that is clear to You."

Then, in the morning, Abraha prepared to enter. The elephant knelt down. They urged it on, but it refused. They beat it, but it refused. They turned it toward Yemen, and it got up running; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; and toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), and it refused. So God sent birds from the sea.

They differed about their description. Ibn 'Abbās said: they had beaks like the beaks of birds and claws like the claws of dogs. 'Ikrimah said: they had heads like the heads of beasts of prey. Ibn Isḥāq said: they were like swallows (al-khaṭāṭīf).

They differed about their colors in three opinions.

The first: they were green. This was said by 'Ikrimah and Sa'īd ibn Jubayr.

The second: they were black. This was said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.

The third: they were white. This was said by Qatādah, who added: each bird had three stones, two in its feet and one in its beak.

They differed about the description of the stones. Some said they were like chickpeas and lentils. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: rather, the stone was like the head of a man or a camel. When they overtook the people, the birds released them upon them, and those stones did not strike anyone without his perishing. A stone would fall on a man's head and come out through his anus. It was also said: each stone bore the name of the one on whom it fell.

(p-235) They perished without entering the Sacred Precinct. God sent upon Abraha a disease in his body, so his fingertips fell off, and his chest split in two, exposing his heart, and he died. The people of Mecca saw the birds coming from the direction of the sea, and 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib said, "These birds are strange." Then 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib sent his son 'Abd Allāh on a horse to look at the people, and he returned galloping and saying, "The people have all perished." 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib and his companions went out and seized their wealth as spoils. It is also said: none of the people escaped except Abū Yaksūm. He set out, and a bird flew above him without his noticing it until he entered upon the Negus and informed him of what had befallen the people. When he finished his speech, the bird struck him and he died. Thus God showed the Negus how his companions had perished.

They differed about how many years were between the birth of the Messenger of God ﷺ and this story, in three opinions.

The first: the Messenger of God ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, and this is the most sound opinion.

(p-236) The second: there were twenty-three years between them. This was related by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn 'Abbās.

The third: forty years. This was related by Muqātil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did He not make their plot﴾, meaning what they intended of destroying the Ka'bah, ﴿into misguidance?﴾, i.e., into loss. The meaning is that their plot went astray from what they aimed at, so they did not reach their goal. ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾.

Regarding "al-abābīl" there are five opinions.

The first: they are scattered from here and there. This was said by Ibn Mas'ūd and al-Akhfash.

The second: they are successive, one following another. This was said by Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid, and Muqātil.

The third: they are numerous. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Ṭāwūs.

The fourth: they are a gathering after a gathering. This was said by 'Aṭā' and Abū Ṣāliḥ, and likewise Abū 'Ubaydah, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjāj said: "al-abābīl" are groups in dispersal.

The fifth: they are of differing colors. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Al-Farrā' and Abū 'Ubaydah said: "al-abābīl" has no singular.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿pelting them﴾. Abū 'Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read "yarmīhim" with the letter yā'. We have already explained the meaning of ﴿sijjīl﴾ in [Hūd: 82], and the meaning of "'aṣf" in [al-Raḥmān: 12], may He be exalted and glorified.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿eaten﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: that it means the grain within it was taken and eaten, and what remained was without grain.

(p-237) The second: that it means "'aṣf" is the food of livestock, just as one says of wheat, "this is the food" though it has not been eaten, and of water, "this is the drink" though it has not been drunk, meaning that both are things that are eaten and drunk. This was mentioned by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: that "the eaten" here refers to that in which devouring occurred. The meaning is: He made them like the leaves of a field that has dried and been eaten, i.e., devoured. This was said by al-Zajjāj.
